chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from al-'Ala', the seller of Sabir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman who deposited wealth with a man. When death approached her, she said to him, 'The wealth that I gave you is for So-and-so.' The woman died, and her heirs came to the man and said, 'There was wealth belonging to our companion which we do not see except with you; swear to us that there is nothing with you.' He would swear to them. He (the Imam) said to them, 'If the woman was trustworthy in your eyes, then swear to them; and if she was suspected (of owing more), then do not swear, and leave the matter as it was. Indeed, she is entitled to one-third of the wealth.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an oath from a custodian when a depositor declares a portion of their wealth near death?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar clarifies the evidentiary weight of a dying declaration (marad al-maut) regarding deposited wealth, distinguishing between a trustworthy depositor (ma'mun) and a suspected one (muttahamah). If the depositor is deemed trustworthy, the custodian must swear an oath to the heirs to retain the full amount; if suspected, the custodian does not swear, and the heirs are limited to receiving only one-third of the wealth. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle that the reliability of the declarant directly impacts the burden of proof and the distribution of the specific asset in question.
